name: STM32H723ZET6
title: STM32H723xE/G Arm Cortex-M7 microcontrollers, 550 MHz, 512 Kbytes or 1 Mbyte Flash, 564 Kbytes RAM, 1.62 V to 3.6 V
summary: A Cortex-M7 microcontroller with a double-precision FPU and 32-Kbyte instruction and data caches, clocked at up to 550 MHz from a 1.62 V to 3.6 V supply through an on-chip LDO. It carries 512 Kbytes (xE) or 1 Mbyte (xG) of ECC Flash and 564 Kbytes of ECC RAM split over TCM, AXI, AHB and backup areas, with an FMC, two Octo-SPI ports with execute-in-place and two SDMMC hosts for external memory. Its peripherals include two 16-bit ADCs and one 12-bit ADC, two DACs, comparators and op amps, Ethernet, a high-speed USB OTG controller, three FDCANs, an LCD-TFT controller, a camera port, CORDIC and filter accelerators and 24 timers, in TFBGA100, LQFP100, LQFP144 and UFBGA144 packages.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M7 with DP-FPU, 550 MHz max, 1177 DMIPS (2.14 DMIPS/MHz)
564 Kbytes with ECC: 128 KB DTCM, 64 KB ITCM, 192 KB ITCM/AXI shared, 128 KB AXI, 3 x 16 KB SRAM1/2/4, 4 KB backup
1.62 V to 3.6 V (1.71 V min with the internal PDR on)
2 x 16-bit up to 3.6 MSPS (7.2 MSPS double-interleaved), 1 x 12-bit up to 5 MSPS
Up to 35 interfaces: 5 I2C, 5 USART + 5 UART + LPUART, 6 SPI (4 I2S), 2 SAI, 3 FDCAN, Ethernet MAC, USB 2.0 HS/FS OTG
24: seventeen 16-bit (5 low-power) and four 32-bit, plus 2 watchdogs and SysTick
TFBGA100 (8 x 8 mm), LQFP100 (14 x 14 mm), LQFP144 (20 x 20 mm), UFBGA144 (7 x 7 mm)

circuits.title: Pin loading conditions
circuits.description: Pin figures are measured into a 50 pF capacitor from the pin to ground.
notes: PA0 stands for any pin.

circuits.title: Current consumption measurement
circuits.description: With the LDO on, the supply current IDD is measured into VDD, VDDLDO and VDDA joined together, and IDD_VBAT separately into VBAT.
notes: VDDLDO, where the package brings it out, is on the VDD net.

circuits.title: 8 MHz crystal on the HSE oscillator
circuits.description: An 8 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator between OSC_IN and OSC_OUT, with a load capacitor from each end to ground and REXT in series on the OSC_OUT side; the feedback resistor RF is inside the part. CL1 and CL2 are high-quality ceramic parts, typically 5 pF to 25 pF and normally equal, picked so that their series value plus about 10 pF of pin and board capacitance makes up the load the crystal is specified for. REXT is chosen for the crystal.
notes: A resonator with built-in capacitors replaces Y1, C1 and C2.
The resonator and its capacitors sit as close to the oscillator pins as possible.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal on the LSE oscillator
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT with a load capacitor from each pin to ground. The feedback resistor is inside; no resistor is fitted across the crystal, and adding one is not allowed. The drive level is set by LSEDRV.
notes: A resonator with built-in capacitors replaces Y1, C1 and C2.
The resonator and its capacitors sit as close to the oscillator pins as possible.

circuits.title: NRST pin protection
circuits.description: A 0.1 µF capacitor from NRST to ground keeps stray pulses from resetting the part, and a push-button to ground gives a manual reset; the pull-up RPU is inside. Whatever drives NRST has to pull it below VIL(NRST) max, or the reset is not taken.

circuits.title: ADC input connection
circuits.description: A source VAIN feeds an ADC input through its own resistance RAIN; the board and the pad add Cparasitic to ground. Inside, the input sees two clamp diodes, a leakage of ±1 µA and the sampling switch RADC with its hold capacitor CADC. RAIN stays within the limit for the resolution in the ADC tables. Cparasitic is the PCB capacitance, which depends on soldering and layout, plus about 5 pF of pad; a large value costs accuracy, and a lower fADC wins it back.

parts.note: PCB plus pad, pad about 5 pF

notes: PA0 stands for any ADC input AINx.

circuits.title: Supply and reference decoupling, VREF+ separate from VDDA
circuits.description: VREF+ and VDDA each take a 1 µF capacitor in parallel with a 100 nF ceramic capacitor to VSSA, placed as close to the part as possible. Where a package has no VREF+ and VREF- pins, they are joined to VDDA and VSSA inside.

circuits.title: Supply and reference decoupling, VREF+ joined to VDDA
circuits.description: With VREF+ tied to VDDA, the joined node takes one 1 µF capacitor in parallel with a 100 nF ceramic capacitor to VREF-/VSSA, placed as close to the part as possible.

circuits.title: DAC output load
circuits.description: The load the DAC is specified into: RL and CL in parallel from DAC_OUTx to ground, driven through the output buffer or with the buffer bypassed by BOFFx in DAC_CR.
notes: PA4 (DAC1_OUT1) stands for either DAC output.

operation.text: Aimed at motor drives and control, medical equipment, industrial gear (PLCs, inverters, circuit breakers), printers and scanners, alarms, video intercoms and HVAC, home audio, mobile and IoT products, and wearables such as smart watches.

Ambient temperature -40 °C to +85 °C. Supply 1.62 V to 3.6 V: below 1.71 V only with PDR_ON tied to VSS and an external power supervisor; with the embedded power-down detector in use VDD must stay above 1.71 V. Separate supply inputs serve the USB transceiver.

Arm Cortex-M7 with an FPU handling single and double precision (IEEE 754) and the DSP instruction set. Six-stage dual-issue pipeline with dynamic branch prediction; Harvard L1 caches of 32 Kbytes each for instructions and data; a 64-bit AXI master, a 64-bit ITCM port, two 32-bit DTCM ports and a low-latency AHB-Lite peripheral port (AHBP). Rated 1177 DMIPS, 2.14 DMIPS/MHz (Dhrystone 2.1), at up to 550 MHz.

The MPU sets access rights and attributes for privileged and user code. Up to 16 regions, each split into up to 8 subregions, from 32 bytes up to the 4-Gbyte space; it is programmed and switched on before use. A forbidden access raises a memory-management exception.

Up to 1 Mbyte of user Flash in eight 128-Kbyte sectors (4 K Flash words each), plus 128 Kbytes of system Flash holding the bootloader and 2 Kbytes (64 Flash words) of user option bytes. A Flash word is 256 bits (8 words, 32 bytes) with 10 ECC bits for single-error correction and double-error detection.

128 to 320 Kbytes of AXI-SRAM on the D1 domain; SRAM1 and SRAM2, 16 Kbytes each, on D2; SRAM4, 16 Kbytes, on D3; 4 Kbytes of backup SRAM, write-protected and kept in Standby and VBAT modes. TCM RAM runs at zero wait states: 64 to 256 Kbytes of ITCM on the 64-bit instruction port and 128 Kbytes of DTCM as two 64-Kbyte banks on the two 32-bit DTCM ports, usable in parallel by the dual-issue core. 192 Kbytes can be given to either AXI-SRAM or ITCM in 64-Kbyte steps. The CPU and the MDMA (also in Sleep mode) reach the TCMs through the core's AHBS slave port.

All SRAM is ECC-protected with a SECDED code: 7 check bits per 32-bit word, 8 per 64-bit word in AXI-SRAM and ITCM-RAM. Bit errors from ageing or radiation are expected over the product life, and application software is meant to handle the ECC events.

The BOOT pin together with the BOOT_ADDx option bytes picks the boot address anywhere from 0x0000 0000 to 0x3FFF FFFF: all of Flash, all RAM (ITCM, DTCM, SRAMs) or the system-memory bootloader. The bootloader reprograms Flash over USART, I2C, SPI, FDCAN or USB-DFU (application note AN2606).

Hardware engine for trigonometric and hyperbolic functions: 24-bit CORDIC rotation, circular and hyperbolic modes, rotation and vectoring. Functions: cosine, sine, cosh, sinh, atan2, atan, atanh, square root, modulus and natural log, with precision programmable up to 20 bits and 4 bits gained per clock. 16-bit or 32-bit fixed-point in and out, an AHB slave port with low latency, results readable as soon as done without polling or interrupt, and DMA read and write channels.

Filter accelerator built on a MAC unit with address generation over a 256 x 16-bit local memory: 16 x 16-bit multiplier, 24+2-bit accumulator that adds and subtracts, 16-bit data in and out. Up to three buffers (two inputs, one output) set by base pointers and sizes, circular if wanted, with a watermark to cut interrupt load. Runs FIR and IIR (direct form 1) filters; AHB slave with DMA read and write channels.

VDD 1.62 V to 3.6 V for the I/Os; VDDLDO 1.62 V to 3.6 V into the regulator that makes VCORE; VDDA 1.62 V to 3.6 V for the ADCs, DACs, comparators and op amps; VDD33USB for the USB transceiver at 3.3 V whatever VDD is; VBAT 1.2 V to 3.6 V for the VSW domain while VDD is missing; VCAP for VCORE, at 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 or 1.35 V set by the VOS bits of PWR_D3CR. VCORE is split into D1 (the core and some peripherals), D2 (most peripherals) and D3 (system control and some peripherals), each able to be switched off on its own.

While VDD is under 1 V, VDDA and VDD33USB must stay below VDD + 300 mV; above 1 V the supplies are independent. On power-down VDD may briefly fall below the other supplies as long as the energy delivered to the device stays under 1 mJ, so that decoupling capacitors can discharge at different rates.

POR holds the device in reset while VDD is under a fixed threshold; PDR resets it when VDD falls under a fixed threshold and is switched on or off by the PDR_ON pin; BOR resets it when VDD falls under one of three thresholds from 2.1 V to 2.7 V chosen in the option bytes.

One regulator feeds D1, D2 and D3; D1 and D2 can be powered down separately. Six output levels: in Run, VOS0 (boosted performance), VOS1 (high performance), VOS2 (medium) and VOS3 (lowest consumption); in Stop, SVOS3, where peripherals able to wake from Stop (UART, SPI, I2C, LPTIM) keep running, and SVOS4/SVOS5, where those peripherals stop but a GPIO or asynchronous interrupt can still wake the device.

Power is saved by lowering clock rates, gating unused peripheral clocks and choosing a low-power mode: CSleep (CPU clock off), CStop (CPU subsystem clock off), DStop (a domain's bus-matrix clock off), Stop (system clock off), DStandby (a domain powered down) and Standby (system powered down). CSleep and CStop start on WFI or WFE, or on return from an interrupt with SLEEPONEXIT set. A domain drops to DStop or DStandby once its processor, subsystem and peripherals are all in low-power mode, and the system goes to Stop or Standby once its domains are in DStop or DStandby and no EXTI wakeup source is pending.

The RCC sits in D3 and handles clock sources, gating and peripheral resets; peripherals with separate bus and kernel clocks keep their baud rate when the system clock changes. Internal oscillators: HSI 64 MHz, HSI48 48 MHz, CSI 4 MHz, LSI 32 kHz. External: HSE 4 to 50 MHz from an external clock or 4 to 48 MHz from a crystal or ceramic resonator, and LSE 32.768 kHz. Three PLLs, one for the system clock and two for kernel clocks. The device starts on HSI.

A power-on reset clears every register; a system reset leaves the debug logic, part of the RCC, the power controller status registers and the backup domain alone. System reset comes from power-on reset, brownout, a low level on NRST, either watchdog, software, a low-power-mode security reset or leaving Standby.

Software makes each pin an input (floating, pull-up or pull-down), an output (push-pull or open-drain, optionally pulled up or down) or an alternate function; most share digital or analog peripheral functions. All are high-current capable with selectable speed. After reset every GPIO except the debug pins is in Analog mode. The configuration can be locked with a set write sequence.

A 64-bit AXI matrix in D1, a 32-bit AHB matrix in D2 and another in D3, joined by bridges. AXI masters: the core (AXIM), SDMMC1, MDMA, DMA2D and LTDC; AXI slaves: Flash, AXI-SRAM, OCTOSPI1/2, FMC and the AHB3/APB3 bridge. D2 AHB masters: DMA1, DMA2, Ethernet MAC, SDMMC2 and USB HS, with SRAM1, SRAM2, AHB1, AHB2, APB1 and APB2 as slaves. D3 holds the BDMA, SRAM4, the backup SRAM, AHB4 and APB4. AXI and AHB buses run at up to 275 MHz, APB buses at up to 138 MHz.

Four DMA engines and a request router. MDMA in D1: 16 channels with single, repeated-block and linked-list transfers, an AXI master and its own AHB path into the TCMs; it can drive the D2 DMAs or serve peripheral requests directly. DMA1 and DMA2 in D2: dual-port with FIFOs (8 streams each). BDMA in D3: basic, with request routing. DMAMUX routes peripheral requests to the controllers and can raise requests from peripheral triggers or DMA events.

Image DMA: fills an area with one colour, copies an image or part of one, converting its colour format if asked, and blends two sources of different formats into a destination of another format. Handles 4-bit to 32-bit colour depths, indexed or direct, including block YCbCr from a JPEG decoder; has its own CLUT memories; interrupts at the end of an operation or at a programmed watermark, and works without the CPU or the DMAs.

16 priority levels, up to 140 maskable interrupt channels besides the core's 16 lines, low-latency entry with the vector address passed straight to the core, late-arrival and tail-chaining handling, and context saved and restored by hardware.

Up to 80 event/interrupt lines: 26 configurable (own pending flag, edge selection, software trigger) and 54 direct (from peripheral status flags). It can wake the core, the power domains or D3 from Stop.
Computes a CRC with a programmable polynomial, for example to check transmitted or stored data, or to compare a run-time signature of the Flash against one made at link time (EN/IEC 60335-1).

External memory controller for SRAM, NOR/OneNAND Flash, PSRAM (4 banks), NAND Flash with hardware ECC over up to 8 Kbytes, and SDRAM/mobile LPSDR SDRAM. 8- or 16-bit data bus, a chip select and configuration per bank, a write FIFO and an SDRAM read FIFO. FMC_CLK/FMC_SDCLK is at most the FMC kernel clock divided by 2.

Two OCTOSPI ports for single, dual, quad or octal SPI memory, multiplexed over shared pins by the OCTOSPIM I/O manager. Modes: indirect (register driven), status polling (periodic read of the memory status with an interrupt on a flag) and memory-mapped (the memory appears in the address map for reads and writes). Frame formats: classic command/address/alternate/dummy/data, and HyperBus. Serves serial PSRAM, NAND and NOR Flash, HyperRAM, HyperFlash and multi-chip packages of them.

Three ADCs: ADC1 and ADC2 at 16 bits (selectable 16, 14, 12, 10 or 8) and ADC3 at 12 bits (12, 10 or 8). Each has up to 20 external channels in single-shot or scan mode, simultaneous or interleaved sample-and-hold, DMA, and an analog watchdog on one, several or all channels that interrupts outside set thresholds. Conversions can be triggered by TIM1, TIM2, TIM3, TIM4, TIM6, TIM8, TIM15, TIM23, TIM24 and LPTIM1. The 16-bit ADCs reach 3.6 MSPS (7.2 MSPS double-interleaved, up to 18 channels); the 12-bit ADC reaches 5 MSPS with up to 12 channels.

An analog sensor whose voltage VTS rises linearly with junction temperature, on ADC3_IN17, for a range of -40 °C to +125 °C with a conversion range of 1.7 V to 3.6 V. Its offset varies between chips, so uncalibrated it suits only relative measurements; each device carries factory calibration values in read-only system memory.
The DTS turns temperature into a square wave whose frequency tracks it, measured against PCLK or LSE; the reference manual gives the formula from the DTS_DR count to temperature.

The backup domain (RTC, backup registers, backup SRAM) runs from VDD when present and switches to the VBAT pin when the PDR sees VDD fall below its level. VBAT may come from a battery, a supercapacitor or VDD itself, in which case VBAT mode does nothing. External interrupts and RTC alarms or events do not end VBAT operation. With PDR_ON at VSS the VBAT function is lost and VBAT is to be tied to VDD.

Two buffered 12-bit channels, each with its own converter: 8- or 12-bit monotonic output, left or right alignment in 12-bit mode, synchronized update, noise and triangle wave generation, independent or simultaneous conversion, DMA with underrun detection per channel, and external triggers (timer update outputs). Reference VREF+ or the internal VREFBUF.

COMP1 and COMP2, rail to rail, with programmable reference, hysteresis, speed (a slow low-power setting) and output polarity. Reference: an I/O, a DAC channel, or the internal reference or 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 of it. They wake the device from Stop, raise interrupts and timer breaks, and pair up as a window comparator.

OPAMP1 and OPAMP2, rail to rail, each with two inputs and an output reachable on pins. Follower or PGA with non-inverting gain 2, 4, 8 or 16, or inverting gain -1, -3, -7 or -15; one positive input can take the DAC, the output can go to an ADC. Input bias current as low as 1 nA, input offset as low as 1.5 mV, GBW reaching 7.3 MHz.

One DFSDM with 4 filters and 8 serial input channels (or 8 internal parallel inputs) for external sigma-delta modulators and PDM microphones (PDM to PCM in hardware). Serial inputs: SPI or Manchester, input clock up to 20 MHz (10 MHz Manchester), clock output 0 to 20 MHz. Parallel inputs up to 16 bits from the ADCs or memory by DMA. Filters: Sinc order 1 to 5 with oversampling up to 1024, integrator oversampling 1 to 256, up to 24-bit signed output, offset correction. Conversions continuous or single, started by software, timers, external events or in step with the first filter; regular and injected conversions. Analog watchdog (Sinc order 1 to 3, oversampling 1 to 32), short-circuit detector counting 1 to 256 equal bits, break outputs, min/max extremes detector, DMA, interrupts and a pulse skipper for beamforming.

8-, 10-, 12- or 14-bit parallel input from camera modules and CMOS sensors, up to 140 Mbyte/s with PIXCLK at 80 MHz. Programmable clock and sync polarity; monochrome or raw Bayer, YCbCr 4:2:2, RGB 565 or compressed data such as JPEG; continuous or snapshot capture; cropping.

Generic 8- or 16-bit synchronous parallel slave port, input or output, with an 8-word (32-byte) FIFO. A data enable input (DE) and a ready output (RDY) give data-valid and flow-control handshakes. It shares circuitry with the DCMI and cannot run at the same time.

24-bit parallel RGB output with all panel signals, up to XGA (1024 x 768). Two layers each with a 64 x 64-bit FIFO and a CLUT of up to 256 colours (256 x 24-bit), up to 8 input colour formats per layer, alpha blending with a per-point or constant alpha, colour keying, up to 4 programmable interrupts, and an AXI master bursting 16 words.

True random number generator giving 32-bit samples of full entropy from an analog noise source and a conditioning stage; usable as an NIST SP 800-90B entropy source; tested with the BSI AIS-31 (T0 to T8) and NIST SP800-90B suites.
Two advanced-control, twelve general-purpose, two basic and five low-power timers, two watchdogs and SysTick. Every timer counter can be frozen while debugging.

TIM1 and TIM8: three-phase PWM over 6 channels with complementary outputs and programmable dead time; 4 channels for input capture, output compare, edge- or centre-aligned PWM and one-pulse output; 0 to 100 % modulation. They link with the other timers for synchronization or chaining and have their own DMA requests.

TIM2, TIM5, TIM23 and TIM24 (32-bit) and TIM3 and TIM4 (16-bit) count up or down with a 16-bit prescaler and 4 channels for capture, compare, PWM or one-pulse, up to 24 channels on the largest packages; they handle quadrature encoders and 1 to 4 Hall sensors and have their own DMA requests. TIM12 and TIM15 (2 channels) and TIM13, TIM14, TIM16 and TIM17 (1 channel) are 16-bit up-counters with a 16-bit prescaler. All can be linked for synchronization.
TIM6 and TIM7 are 16-bit time bases, mainly for DAC triggering and waveform generation, with their own DMA requests.

LPTIM1 to LPTIM5 keep counting in Stop mode on LSE, LSI or an external clock and can wake the device. 16-bit up-counter with 16-bit auto-reload and compare, pulse or PWM output, continuous or one-shot, software or hardware trigger, clock from LSE, LSI, HSI, APB or an external input (counting even with no internal clock running), digital glitch filter and encoder mode.

12-bit down-counter with an 8-bit prescaler on its own 32 kHz RC, so it runs in Stop and Standby; used as a watchdog or a free-running timeout timer, started by hardware or software per the option bytes, with a window option that resets on a reload made too early.
7-bit down-counter on the main clock with an early-warning interrupt; it can be frozen while debugging.
24-bit down-counter with auto-reload, a maskable interrupt at zero and a programmable clock source, meant for an RTOS tick.

BCD calendar with sub-seconds, seconds, minutes, hours (12/24), weekday, date, month and year, with automatic month-length and leap-year correction. Two alarms; shift correction of 1 to 32767 RTC clock pulses; 50/60 Hz reference clock input; digital calibration in 0.95 ppm steps; three tamper pins with a filter; timestamp on a pin event, tamper or switch to VBAT; 17-bit wakeup timer. The RTC and 32 backup registers (128 bytes, kept through system reset, power reset and Standby wakeup) run from VDD or VBAT. Clock: LSE crystal, external LSE resonator or oscillator, LSI (32 kHz typ) or HSE/32. On LSE it works in VBAT and every low-power mode; on LSI it works in the low-power modes but not in VBAT mode. Alarm, wakeup, timestamp and tamper events interrupt and wake the device.

Five I2C interfaces to I2C-bus spec rev. 5: master, slave and multimaster; Standard 100 kbit/s, Fast 400 kbit/s, Fast-mode Plus 1 Mbit/s with 20 mA drive; 7- and 10-bit and multiple 7-bit addresses; programmable setup and hold; optional clock stretching. SMBus 2.0 (hardware PEC, ARP, alert) and PMBus 1.1. Independent kernel clock, wakeup from Stop on address match, programmable analog and digital filters against noise, and a 1-byte data buffer served by DMA.

USART1, USART2, USART3, USART6 and USART10 plus UART4, UART5, UART7, UART8 and UART9: asynchronous, IrDA SIR, multiprocessor, single-wire half duplex, LIN master/slave, CTS/RTS and RS485 driver enable, up to 12.5 Mbit/s. The USARTs add Smartcard (ISO 7816) and SPI-like modes. Transmit and receive FIFOs, off by default. Each has a clock independent of the CPU and can wake the device from Stop on a start bit, any frame, a chosen frame or a FIFO state; all work with DMA.

LPUART1: low-power asynchronous serial with half-duplex single wire, CTS/RTS, multiprocessor mode and TX/RX FIFOs (off by default). Its own clock domain lets it wake the device from Stop on a start bit, any frame, a chosen frame or a FIFO state. On the 32.768 kHz LSE alone it reaches 9600 baud, so it can wait for frames in Stop; a faster clock gives higher rates. DMA capable.

Six SPIs (SPI2S1, SPI2S2, SPI2S3, SPI4, SPI5, SPI2S6) at up to 150 Mbit/s as master or slave, full duplex, half duplex or simplex; 3-bit prescaler for 8 master rates; frames of 4 to 16 bits; NSS pulse mode, TI mode, hardware CRC and 8 x 8-bit RX and TX FIFOs with DMA. Four I2S interfaces share SPI1, SPI2, SPI3 and SPI6: master or slave, simplex, 16- or 32-bit (SPI2S6 16-bit only), 8 kHz to 192 kHz sampling, master clock out at 256 x fs, 16 x 8-bit FIFOs with DMA. An internal audio PLL or an external clock gives audio-grade accuracy.

SAI1 and SAI4, each with two independent audio sub-blocks having their own clock generator and I/O control: I2S, LSB/MSB justified, PCM/DSP, TDM, AC'97, and SPDIF output when transmitting. Up to 192 kHz sampling; PDM interface for up to 8 microphones; master or slave; sub-blocks transmit or receive, synchronously or not; SAIs can be synchronized together.

S/PDIF receiver to IEC-60958 and IEC-61937 (stereo up to high rates, compressed surround up to 5.1): up to 4 inputs, automatic symbol-rate detection up to 12.288 MHz, 32 kHz to 192 kHz stereo, parity handling, DMA for samples and for control/user channel data, interrupts. It decodes the Manchester stream into frames, sub-frames and blocks and gives a spdif_frame_sync signal at the sub-frame rate for clock-drift tracking.
Single Wire Protocol master (the CLF side of ETSI TS 102 613): full duplex, automatic bus state handling (active, suspend, resume), bit rate up to 2 Mbit/s, automatic SOF, EOF and CRC, DMA capable.

MDIO slave with 32 register addresses, each with a 16-bit output register (firmware read/write, MDIO read) and a 16-bit input register (firmware read, MDIO write); configurable port address; maskable interrupts on register write, register read and protocol error; works in and wakes from Stop.
Two SD/SDIO/MMC hosts, one card each: MMC 4.51 with 1-, 4- or 8-bit bus; SD memory 4.1 and SDIO 4.0 with 1- or 4-bit bus; a built-in DMA for transfers to SRAM.

FDCAN1, FDCAN2 and FDCAN3 meet ISO 11898-1 (CAN 2.0 A and B) and CAN FD 1.0. FDCAN1 adds time-triggered CAN (ISO 11898-4) with global time and drift compensation. A shared 10-Kbyte message RAM holds filters, RX FIFOs and buffers, TX event FIFOs and TX buffers. An optional clock calibration unit can derive a calibrated CAN clock from HSI and the PLL using frames received on FDCAN1.

USB 2.0 and OTG 2.0 device/host/OTG controller: full speed (12 Mbit/s) through the on-chip PHY, high speed (480 Mbit/s) through an external ULPI PHY (12 signals, clocked from its 60 MHz output, SDR). Needs a 48 MHz clock from a PLL on HSE. 4-Kbyte shared RX/TX FIFO sized dynamically, SRP and HNP, 8 endpoints usable both ways, 16 host channels (periodic OUT supported), OTG 1.3/2.0 selectable, LPM, Battery Charging 1.2, internal DMA, no external resistors needed. A power switch is needed in host or OTG mode when bus-powered devices attach.

IEEE 802.3-2002 MAC with its own DMA, to an external PHY over MII (17 signals) or RMII (9 signals); the device can supply the PHY's 25 MHz clock in MII. 10 and 100 Mbit/s, VLAN tags, half duplex (CSMA/CD) and full duplex, control frames, 32-bit CRC insertion and removal, address filtering, 32-bit status per frame, 2-Kbyte TX and RX FIFOs, and IEEE 1588-2008 (PTP v2) time stamping with the comparator wired to TIM2 and an interrupt when system time passes a target.
Hardware for the HDMI Consumer Electronics Control protocol, a slow control link between audio/video products. It has its own clock domain and can wake the device from Stop when data arrives.

JTAG and serial-wire debug ports, breakpoints, code-execution trace, software instrumentation, trigger input and output, serial-wire trace and a trace port (TRACECLK, TRACED[3:0]) on Arm CoreSight components, with a 2-Kbyte embedded trace buffer.
Peripheral boundary addresses and the memory map are given in the reference manual (RM0468).

FT pins tolerate 5 V and TT pins 3.3 V. Suffixes: _f I2C Fast-mode Plus, _a analog function supplied from VDDA, _u USB function supplied from VDD33USB, _h high-speed low-voltage. PC2_C and PC3_C are analog-only pads (TT_a) on the TFBGA100, LQFP100 and LQFP144; the UFBGA144 instead has PC2 and PC3 as full I/Os.

Voltages are referred to VSS. Minimum and maximum values hold over the worst junction temperature, supply and frequency; they are tested on every part at TJ = 25 °C and at the TJmax of its temperature range. Values marked as coming from characterization, simulation or design are mean ± 3σ of sample tests. Typical values are at TJ = 25 °C and VDD = 3.3 V, are design guides and are not tested. Typical ADC accuracy figures are met by 95 % of parts (mean ± 2σ), from a lot characterized over the full temperature range. Typical curves are design guides and are not tested.
Pin parameters are measured with a 50 pF load from the pin to ground; an input voltage is the voltage between the pin and ground.

VDD powers the I/Os, the HSI, CSI, HSI48 and HSE oscillators and the PLLs, the VBAT charger and the power switch that feeds the backup domain from VDD or VBAT (VSW). VDDLDO feeds the LDO regulator, whose output VCORE (on VCAP) powers the core domain: D3 (system logic, EXTI, peripherals, RAM) directly, and D2 (peripherals, RAM) and D1 (CPU, peripherals, RAM, Flash) through their own power switches. The backup domain holds the LSI, LSE, RTC, wakeup logic, backup registers and reset; the backup RAM is fed through a backup regulator and a power switch. VDD33USB powers the USB FS I/Os. VDDA, with VREF+ and VREF- and their return VSSA, powers REF_BUF, the ADCs and DACs, and the op amps and comparators.
Supply current is measured with the LDO on: IDD flows into VDD, VDDLDO and VDDA tied together, and IDD_VBAT into VBAT alone.

Going past the absolute maximum voltage, current or thermal ratings can damage the part for good. They are stress limits only: the part is not meant to work at them, and long exposure to them can shorten its life. The mission profile follows JEDEC JESD47; longer mission profiles can be had on request.

The LDO is kept stable by an external capacitor CEXT on VCAP: 2.2 µF with ESR below 100 mΩ, and two such capacitors may sit on the VCAP pins. A real capacitor behaves as its capacitance with an ESR in series and a leakage resistance across it. When the regulator is bypassed, each 2.2 µF is replaced by 100 nF of decoupling.

The current depends on supply voltage, temperature, pin loading, software configuration, clock frequencies, how fast the pins switch, where the program sits in memory and what code runs. Run-mode figures are taken with CoreMark, all I/Os in analog input mode, peripherals off unless stated, Flash wait states at the minimum for fACLK, and, with peripherals on, an AHB clock of half the CPU clock and an APB clock of half the AHB clock.

An input with pull-up draws current whenever the pin is held low outside, as set by the pull resistor values; an output's external pull-down or load adds its own current. An input sitting at a level between the thresholds draws current through its Schmitt trigger; pins not used as digital inputs, and ADC inputs in particular, are set to analog mode to avoid it. A floating input can drift to such a level or toggle from outside noise, so unused pins are set to analog mode, held by a pull resistor, or set as outputs.
A switching pin draws current from the supply for its own circuitry and to charge and discharge the capacitance on it, internal and external, in proportion to supply voltage, frequency and load.

Wakeup times run from the wakeup event to the first instruction the CPU executes. Stop and Sleep are left on a WFE; the WKUP pin PC1 wakes the part from Standby, Stop and Sleep. Measured at VDD = 3.3 V.

In bypass mode the HSE or LSE oscillator is off and OSC_IN or OSC32_IN acts as a standard input, so the external clock meets the I/O static characteristics; the recommended waveform has the levels and times of the external clock tables.

The HSE runs from a 4 MHz to 50 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator. The figures come from characterization with the typical parts in the HSE table. Resonator and load capacitors sit as close to the oscillator pins as possible, which keeps output distortion and start-up time down. CL1 and CL2 are high-quality ceramic capacitors for high frequency, typically 5 pF to 25 pF, usually of equal value; the crystal's specified load capacitance is their series value, with the pin and board capacitance counted in (about 10 pF as a rough figure).

The LSE runs from a 32.768 kHz crystal or ceramic resonator, characterized with the typical parts of the LSE table; resonator and capacitors sit as close to the pins as possible. No resistor may be fitted between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT.
The Flash memory figures hold at TJ = –40 to 125 °C unless stated. Parts leave the factory with the Flash erased.

Susceptibility is tested on samples while the part runs a simple program toggling two LEDs. ESD of both polarities is applied to every pin until the program is upset (IEC 61000-4-2), and fast transient bursts of both polarities are coupled onto VDD and VSS through 100 pF (IEC 61000-4-4); a reset brings normal operation back. Pins wired to tracks longer than 50 mm, which pick up noise, are best given a 1 kΩ series resistor placed close to the part.

EMC is characterized at component level with a simple program, and the result depends heavily on the application and its software. The software handles runaway cases: a corrupted program counter, an unexpected reset, corrupted critical data such as control registers. Most such failures can be reproduced by holding NRST or the oscillator pins low for one second, and ESD can be applied to the part within its ratings; software that misbehaves under these trials can be hardened against unrecoverable faults.
Emission is measured while the part runs EEMBC code, by the IEC 61967-2 method, which fixes the test board and pin loading.

ESD is applied as a positive then a negative pulse to the pins of each sample, in every pin combination, by ANSI/ESDA/JEDEC JS-001 (human body model) and JS-002 (charged device model). Latch-up is tested on six parts by JESD78: an overvoltage on each supply pin and an injected current into every I/O, input and output pin.
Every I/O except BOOT0 is CMOS and TTL compliant with no configuration needed, and covers more than the strict CMOS or TTL limits.

A GPIO sinks or sources up to ±8 mA, or up to ±20 mA with relaxed VOL and VOH. The number of pins driving current is limited so that the current sourced by all I/Os plus the Run current of the MCU stays within ΣIVDD, and the current sunk stays within ΣIVSS.
The HSLV bit in SYSCFG_CCCSR speeds up the I/Os when the supply is below 2.7 V.
The NRST input is CMOS with a permanent pull-up RPU, followed by a filter before the internal reset.
In the FMC timing tables Tfmc_ker_ck is the period of fmc_ker_ck. In asynchronous mode 1 FMC_NADV is not used; it appears in modes 2/B, C and D.

A negative current injected into any analog input markedly worsens the accuracy of a conversion on another analog input; a Schottky diode from pin to ground on inputs that may inject negative current is recommended. Positive injection within IINJ(PIN) and ΣIINJ(PIN) leaves ADC accuracy unchanged.

Total unadjusted error ET is the largest gap between the actual and ideal transfer curves. Offset error EO compares the first transition of the actual curve with the ideal first transition. Gain error EG compares the ideal last transition with the actual last one. Differential linearity error ED is the largest gap between an actual step and the ideal step. Integral linearity error EL is the largest gap between any actual transition and the line joining the end points.

VDDA and VREF+ are decoupled with 1 µF in parallel with 100 nF of good ceramic, as close to the part as possible, either on each pin when VREF+ is separate or on the joined node when VREF+ is tied to VDDA.
Each DAC output has an optional internal buffer. With it on, the output impedance is low enough to drive an external load with no op amp added; the BOFFx bit in DAC_CR bypasses it.

The I2C meets the I2C-bus specification (revision 03) in Standard-mode (100 kbit/s), Fast-mode (400 kbit/s) and Fast-mode Plus (1 Mbit/s), by design, when it is configured correctly and i2c_ker_ck is above the minimum for the mode. SDA and SCL are not true open-drain: in open-drain mode the PMOS to VDDIOx is off but still there. The 20 mA drive of Fast-mode Plus is not supported, which limits the load capacitance in Fm+. Every SDA and SCL pin has an analog spike filter.

Four packages, all ECOPACK: LQFP100 (14 x 14 mm body, 0.5 mm lead pitch), TFBGA100 (8 x 8 mm, 100 balls at 0.8 mm pitch), LQFP144 (20 x 20 mm, 0.5 mm lead pitch) and UFBGA144 (7 x 7 mm, 144 balls at 0.50 mm pitch).

The top face carries the product identification (for example STM32H723 over VGT6 on LQFP100, VGH6 on TFBGA100, 723ZGI6 under STM32H on UFBGA144), a date code of year (Y) and week (WW), a revision code (R) and a dot at pin 1 or ball A1. Markings vary with the supply chain, and further optional marks may appear. A part marked ES or E, or shipped with an engineering-sample notice, is not qualified for production use.

Junction temperature is worked out from the ambient temperature, the total dissipation (internal power IDD × VDD plus the power in the output pins) and the package's ΘJA. Junction-to-ambient resistance is 43.8 °C/W for LQFP100, 43.2 °C/W for TFBGA100 and 44.8 °C/W for LQFP144; UFBGA144 is not yet characterised. The figures follow JESD51-2 (still air); ST application note AN5036 covers thermal management for STM32 parts.
